signals.text: Hello. I'm bumping into this when using `fdbcli` inside my `podman` container: ``` bash-5.1# fdbcli Using cluster file `/etc/foundationdb/fdb.cluster'. It looks like this happens when I mount the container and the podman `--envfile` contains the env variable `FDB_TLS_VERIFY_PEERS`. When I mount an envfile that doesn't contain that var fdbcli works. signals.title: Convert `BenchIONet2.actor.cpp` to standard coroutines
signals.text: ## Summary Keep ACTOR and C++20 coroutine versions of `BenchIONet2` in the same `fdbrpc_bench` binary for reproducible comparisons, and fix a remaining lifetime mismatch in the conversion. The ACTOR's `state Reference<IAsyncFile> f` survives loop iterations, so subsequent opens reuse the cached file. A loop-local coroutine handle instead closes the file after each iteration, causing another atomic create, rename, and directory sync. Both implementations now retain the file handle and child futures across iterations and use the same fixed seed. The coroutine child's existing `NoThrowOnCancel` behavior is unchanged. ## Measured results Release build with Clang 19.1.5, libc++, and `-O3`; no sanitizers or profiling. One binary contained ACTOR, the fixed coroutine, and a temporary unfixed coroutine differing only in file-handle lifetime. Six counterbalanced paired rounds produced 126 samples, each in a fresh process. Iteration counts matched across all three implementations at each size. The table reports **launched-child throughput per network-thread CPU second**. Gains compare the fixed and unfixed coroutines; ratios are medians of the six paired rounds. | Batch size | Iterations per sample | Throughput gain from fix | Fixed / ACTOR throughput | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 64 | +3.7% | 1.004x | | 8 | 64 | +34.7% | 1.000x | | 64 | 64 | +34.8% | 0.998x | | 512 | 64 | +29.9% | 0.991x | | 4,096 | 16 | +32.5% | 0.994x | | 32,768 | 8 | +22.5% | 0.720x | | 65,536 | 8 | +18.5% | 0.419x | The fix improved all 42 paired comparisons and restored approximate ACTOR parity through batch size 4,096. A substantial gap remains at the two largest sizes. At 65,536, the gain ranged from 17.7% to 20.2%, while fixed/ACTOR ranged from 0.377x to 0.568x. These are observed ranges, not confidence bounds. ## Validation - The final patch compiled successfully. ACTOR and coroutine smoke cases at sizes 1 and 65,536 passed (4/4). - A separate instrumented call-count check at size 512 with 16 iterations observed one atomic-file open, rename, and directory sync for ACTOR and the fixed coroutine, versus 16 of each for the unfixed coroutine. All three performed 16 data syncs. - The temporary unfixed variant and fixed-iteration controls were removed from the final patch. The instrumented call-count check and final smoke timings are excluded from the performance table. This fixes a benchmark-workload mismatch, not the entire large-batch slowdown. Retained backlog depends on both batch size and iteration count; extra I/O waits can allow more child CPU work to execute, and terminal child cancellation is outside the timed loop. These results do not isolate coroutine-creation cost, establish the cause of the remaining gap, or measure production performance. They are a controlled comparison on the updated source, not a reproduction of the historical table's exact environment.

signals.title: Surface degraded multi-region status when failover is stuck waiting on the unavailable remote DC #12071
signals.text: **Surface degraded multi-region status when failover is stuck waiting on the unavailable remote DC** This PR introduces observability for #12071. Instead of preventing the stall where recovery waits for an unavailable remote datacenter, this change surfaces the stuck state to improve cluster visibility. ### Key Changes #### New Status Flag: `cluster.degraded_multi_region` The flag becomes `true` when all of the following conditions are met: - The cluster is configured with `usable_regions > 1`. - Recovery has progressed to or beyond the `accepting_commits` stage. - The remote region's log set cannot be recruited (signaled by `RemoteRegionLogsMissing` from `trackTlogRecovery`). - The state persists for longer than `DEGRADED_MULTI_REGION_MIN_STALL_SECONDS` (to avoid false positives during transient windows of normal non-initial recovery). #### New Trace Event - Added `ClusterControllerRecoveryRemoteRegionStall` for improved debugging and monitoring. #### Improved `fdbcli` Output - The data-loss warning is **softened** when `degraded_multi_region` is true, because committed data remains safe in the surviving region. - For empty `id` or `address` fields, the CLI now prints `"unknown"` instead of leaving them blank. #### Testing - **Simulation Test:** `DegradedMultiRegionStatus` – covers the stuck state and includes a false-positive check to ensure healthy recovery doesn't trigger the flag. - **Unit Tests:** Added for the new signal parsing logic. ### Why This Matters In a multi-region configuration, when one region fails, the second (surviving) region first recovers missing data from the **satellite of the first (failed) region**, which remains operational. After this data copy completes, recovery proceeds to the `accepting_commits` stage. However, at this point the recovery may stall because the failed region's logs remain unreachable. While this prevents the remote region from fully recovering, the surviving region continues to accept commits, and all committed data remains safe and consistent. The stall only affects the ability to restore the failed region, not the integrity of committed data. Previously, `fdbcli status` showed a misleading "potential data loss" warning. This PR replaces that with an honest representation of the **degraded but non-data-losing** state, providing clear visibility into the actual cluster condition. --- **Related Issue:** #12071 **Forum Discussion:** [link](https://forums.foundationdb.org/t/3dc2regions-simulating-primary-datacenter-failure/3329/18)

signals.title: (Backport to 7.4): DD finishMoveKeys: move waitForShardReady outside transaction (#13364)
signals.text: Backport 0887ae6d29 from main to release-7.4 ``` ## Backport notes - Branch `release-7.4` uses Flow actors (`.actor.cpp`, `state` keyword, `wait()` macro) rather than main's C++20 coroutines (`co_await`). Local variables that need to cross a `wait()` point are declared with `state`; return statements use `return`, not `co_return`. - `constexpr` is not compatible with `state` variables on 7.4. - Otherwise the change is behavior-identical to the main PR. ``` DD finishMove*: drop the transaction across waitForShardReady SERVER_READY_QUORUM_TIMEOUT (15s) was used inside a transaction with a ~5s lifetime (MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS). When destination servers were slow to respond, the wait alone consumed the txn budget, and commits failed with transaction_too_old — retries too, cascading into the DD pipeline stalls observed in incidents. Restructure both finish-move functions (finishMoveKeys / finishMoveShards, dispatched on SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA) into a two-transaction pattern with the wait in between: Transaction 1: read keyServers / serverTags / serverList (and dataMove metadata for finishMoveShards) via the new readShardState() helper. Save the read version and drop the transaction (tr.reset()). Wait: waitForShardReady — runs OUTSIDE any transaction; the 15s timeout is now safe. Transaction 2: re-verify via destUnchanged() (dest hasn't changed, dataMove still in Running phase for finishMoveShards), then commit metadata writes. If the destination changed during the wait, the inner loop retries from the top — same as today's behaviour on transient errors, just without burning the txn budget on the wait itself. Verification & retry details: * destUnchanged() loops every sub-range, not just keyServers[0]. The keys-flavor (`expectedDataMoveId={}`) tolerates empty-dest entries whose src ⊆ expectedDest — matching the planning loop's `alreadyMoved = dest2.empty() && isSubset` branch, which lets sibling iterations of OUR move that already completed pass through. A foreign src on an empty-dest entry signals a different move owns the range and forces a retry to avoid clobbering it. The shards-flavor uses the dataMoveId stamp as the per-sub-range invariant. * All retry paths (dest-changed, data-move-deleted, phase-changed, plus the count-mismatch else-branch in finishMoveShards) are bounded by FINISH_MOVE_KEYS_MAX_RETRIES and back off via finishMoveKeysBackoff(). Without the cap the dest-changed branch could livelock; the shards- side count-mismatch path was previously unbounded. * Txn 2's writes use the post-wait snapshot: keyServersValue uses reread.uidToTagMap; finishMoveShards introduces a postWaitDataMove local so the partial-complete / deleteCheckpoints / dataMoveValue writes reflect the fresh dataMove state. * runPreCheck=false is set inline on each retry path. The partial-complete success-continue deliberately leaves runPreCheck alone so chunks 2..N of a multi-transaction move each get their own AUDIT_DATAMOVE_PRE_CHECK. * finishMoveShards now takes finishMoveKeysParallelismLock per iteration (mirroring finishMoveKeys). The lock had been function- scoped and released mid-iteration before the wait, so retries ran lockless and silently exceeded MOVE_KEYS_PARALLELISM. * taskID = TaskPriority::MoveKeys is restored on txn 2 in both functions (tr.reset() drops it). * New CODE_PROBEs ("dest changed", "data move deleted", "phase changed") are marked probe::decoration::rare; reaching them requires a concurrent reassignment racing into the wait window. * SHARD_READY_DELAY is buggified to 5.0s to exercise the slow-dest scenario in simulation. Validation: * k8s rig: 3 transaction_too_old events vs 360,289 in the prior run without the patch; 0 OOMs. * Simulation (DDPipelineStall.toml, knob ON): cascade trigger eliminated; transaction_too_old goes to zero; residual TryFinishMoveShardsError events are not_committed which retry cleanly. ` 20260701-232737-stack-backport-74-028aaba11a9b3a30 compressed=True data_size=41562049 duration=3423521 ended=100000 fail_fast=10 max_runs=100000 pass=100000 priority=100 remaining=0 runtime=0:29:46 sanity=False started=100000 stopped=20260701-235723 submitted=20260701-232737 timeout=5400 username=stack-backport-74 `

signals.title: Reduce coroutine overhead on storage-server paths
signals.text: ## Summary Reduce coroutine, allocation, and reference-counting overhead on the storage-server read/write and RPC paths: - Fast-path ready storage/MVCC and Redwood reads without constructing unnecessary coroutine frames or futures. - Cache ready Redwood page futures while preserving pending-future cancellation and lifetime behavior. - Return KAIO write completion directly as `Future<Void>`, avoiding an extra `success()` actor per disk write. - Reduce RPC serialization, `FutureStream`, `ActorCollection`, and detached-sender overhead. - Add focused regression and microbenchmark coverage. ## Performance Re-ran the full PR against main on 2026-08-21: clean main `9d4a14faf451` versus this PR's clean source state. **Observed throughput increased by 10.50% in this matched pair.** These results replace the earlier shorter-run measurements. Both runs used fresh three-process, single-redundancy `ssd-redwood-1` clusters (one stateless, one log, one storage process) on the same x86-64 host with 16 logical CPUs available. Builds used the same Release Clang 19.1.5/libc++/jemalloc configuration, with sanitizers and profiling disabled; source and fresh server/client binary provenance were verified for each revision. Mixed Mako `g18ui` workload: 18 GETs, one update, and one insert per transaction; 100,000 initial rows; 128-byte keys and 512-byte values; four load processes; seven run processes with 16 worker threads and 32 async workflows **per process** (224 workflows total), with no client TPS cap. Each run used `--warmup_seconds 300 --seconds 900`: approximately five minutes of excluded warmup followed by ten measured minutes. Inserts grow the dataset beyond the initial row count. | Revision | Measured TPS | Change vs. main | Conflicts | Errors / timeouts | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Main `9d4a14faf451` | 2,762.39 | — | 41,650 | 0 / 0 | | PR #13699 | **3,052.49** | **+10.50%** | 46,642 | 0 / 0 | Main completed 1,656,401 successful transactions in 599.626 measured seconds; the PR completed 1,830,287 in 599.604 seconds. Storage-server GET-query throughput rose from approximately 53.8k/s to 59.5k/s. Both runs saturated the storage main thread at approximately one CPU core, and every measured ratekeeper observation identified the storage write queue as the limiter. Mean storage queues remained high (approximately 944 MiB on main and 941 MiB on the PR). Mean durability lag was 84.7M versus 76.5M versions, but lag increased during both measurement windows. This is one sequential run per revision on a growing dataset under queue-limited saturation; it does not establish statistical confidence, low-lag steady-state capacity, or the contribution of any individual optimization. Sampled **full-run** latency means, including warmup, computed from exported latency sums/counts across all async workflows: | Operation | Main mean (ms) | PR mean (ms) | Change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | GET | 3.802 | 3.401 | -10.56% | | COMMIT | 3.075 | 3.369 | +9.55% | | TRANSACTION | 77.151 | 70.065 | -9.19% | Transaction and GET means improved in this pair, while the COMMIT mean increased. These are not measurement-only latency statistics. p95/p99 comparisons are omitted because the existing Mako async sketch export retains only the last workflow's sketch per process, rather than all workflows.

signals.title: DD: config-driven bounded-time rollback of shard-encoded location metadata
signals.text: (Rewrite of the description after a request to move this PR to be totally configuration based which makes the PR better but meant more change. Intent is to backport this to 7.4.) Rolling SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA true->false could not reach `audit_storage metadata_encoding` ROLLBACK COMPLETE in bounded time: converged and "safe to downgrade binary" was unverifiable short of a storage wiggle (hours-to-days). This adds an opt-in, bounded-time DD-init rewrite that converges existing keyServers AND serverKeys back to old format and clears DataMoveMetaData, driven by two new DatabaseConfiguration options: configure shard_metadata_format = original | encoded (target format) configure shard_metadata_migration = enabled | disabled (run rewrite) Config is the source of truth for DD's encoding target, resolved once at init as `shard_metadata_format ?? SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA` (the knob is only the fallback when the config is UNSET) and used across all DD write/move paths -- so a rollback is driven by `configure shard_metadata_format=original` with no knob flip and no process restart (the configure triggers a recovery that re-inits DD). Deploying the binary is a byte-identical no-op until an operator opts in. A completion sentinel records ROLLBACK COMPLETE and fast-paths later inits. serverKeys are rewritten serially per storage server, so rewrite time scales with cluster size (minutes typically); progress is visible via DDShardEncode* trace events and the audit. Caveats (details in design/shard-encode-location-metadata.md and documentation/sphinx/source/command-line-interface.rst): - Binary downgrade: a pre-config binary reads only the knob, so downgrade is safe only at ROLLBACK COMPLETE with the target binary deployed SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA=false. - Known limitation: large teams (ddLargeTeamEnabled) and physical shard (ENABLE_DD_PHYSICAL_SHARD), mutually exclusive with shard encoding, still read the raw knob, not the config. Once shard_metadata_format is set, don't move the knob except for a downgrade. Tested: sim tests/fast/ShardEncodeRollback.toml (knob-fallback path) and tests/fast/ShardEncodeRollbackConfig.toml (config-only, no knob flip), each passing a 100,000-run joshua ensemble; plus a live-cluster forward->rollback->re-forward under mako load with DD-pod kills (test_shardencode_rollover_load, fdb-kubernetes-tests). Builds on #13310 (SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA audit + rollback support). Depends on #13670 (audit_storage counting fix, merged) to observe ROLLBACK COMPLETE. Here are two test runs. The first is just exercising the new test. signals.title: Preserve failed-team recovery under DD pipeline back-pressure
signals.text: ## Summary - Prevent ordinary shard relocations from hiding exclusion and failed-team recovery requests behind a saturated admission pipeline. Keep consuming input, reserve one recovery slot within the configured limit, and let cancellations through. - Preserve split, health, and destination-retry intent when coalescing identical ranges, without dropping partial overlaps or durable restored moves. - Account for new admissions against completed queue mutations so pending-to-queued and queued-to-active counter transfers cannot expose temporary capacity to reentrant admissions. ## Validation - Clang builds of `fdbserver_datadistributor_test` and `fdbserver` completed successfully. - Seven pipeline-gate regression tests passed in both normal and simulated modes. - The complete data-distributor unit suite passed: 60 tests, zero failures. - The new production gate/consumer regression fails without the accounting fix (1,001 relocations admitted with a limit of 1,000) and passes with it. - Six unchanged simulation runs passed: four `tests/fast/DDPipelineSaturation.toml` cases and two `tests/slow/DDBalanceAndRemove.toml` cases, with fault injection enabled, zero severe trace errors, pipeline-full coverage, and successful final quiescence.

signals.title: [release-7.3] always increment finishedQueries counter if incrementing allQueries
signals.text: Storage server processes publish a pair of counters `total_queries` and `finished_queries` (as well as a derived special counter `query_queue_max`) tracking how many read operations have been started and finished (and the high-water-mark for the number of pending queries—those that have been started, but not finished—in a status-fetch interval). Unfortunately, the counter underlying `total_queries` was incremented at the beginning of one of several actors, and the matching increment to `finished_queries` was done at the end, with several intervening `wait`s. If the actor was cancelled (or experienced another non-returnable error), `finished_queries` was not incremented, resulting in a permanent drift between `total_queries` and `all_queries` and apparently endless growth in `query_queue_max`. The easiest way to demonstrate this behavior is to have two different clients alternate between setting watches and updating values for the same keys—for example, run two simultaneous instances of this [simple Java program](https://gist.github.com/jkt-signal/1c3ea2a4a6aafd51571b462c57b50fd9) against a single database, and monitor its status to see `query_queue_max` on storage servers go up permanently every time you run the test. To solve this problem, we add a simple class `CountedSection` to `flow/Stats.h` to bump two counters in RAII-enforced balance; once a local `CountedSection` has bumped the first counter, it will always eventually bump the second one whether it is destroyed as a result of normal exit or exception. (Of course, if you store one in a heap object and leak it, you will still experience drift, so, uh, don't do that.) `CountedSection` is made move-only so you can use it in actor state, since `state` variables seem to always be default-constructed and then assigned to their initializers even if the initialization comes before the first `wait` in an actor. One of the actors involved actually updates a second counter pair, `getMappedRangeQueries` and `finishedGetMappedRangeQueries`, in a way vulnerable to the same problem, so we use `CountedSection` to address that as well, though I have not seen any instances of these getting out of sync (entirely due to lack of trying). Some other metrics updated at the ends of the affected actors—mostly latency metrics, but also some tagged size distributions—are not addressed by this change. Arguably they should not be, since including latency and response size of interrupted queries may significantly throw off the statistics in a not-necessarily-useful way. Leaving this as an RFC because I'm not sufficiently familiar with the FoundationDB testing setup to write a good test; the Java program linked above is a great demonstration but is not trivially adapted to an integration test (and presumably we'd like tests of the fdbserver itself to be C++, not dependent on the Java bindings). Advice for how to test the change greatly appreciated! This PR is against the 7.3 branch, rather than `main`, because all the relevant actors have been rewritten to use C++20 standard coroutines in the interim, and while I strongly suspect the same bug applies equally in `main`, I was not able to confirm this because `main` does not currently build a usable fdb for me. Porting forward to `main` should be relatively trivial and I'm happy to do so if requested.

signals.title: Add ipv6 support to docker container
signals.text: Added functionality for `fdb.bash` to support ipv6, provided the new env variable `FDB_IP_VERSION` is set to 6 (or any string containing 6, such as v6, ipv6, iwantipv6, etc. ) There is an unfortunate caveat of no dual stack support, as FDB coordinators are recognized by their IP+port and not their machineid, to the best of my knowledge. If I'm wrong and FDB does not double count a coordinator with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in the cluster file, I would be happy to add dual stack support to this. This was part of now-split-up #13822, with slightly more robust logic. # Changes ## IPv6 Support ### Issue Before now, `fdb.bash` would throw an error if `hostname -i` resolved to a v6 address, as it would not be encased in brackets. ### New Behavior Depending on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, `fdb.bash` will try and find the machine's v4 or v6 address. IPv4 is the default pick. If `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` or `FDB_LISTEN_IP` are set, they will _not_ be overwritten. Otherwise, the first IPv4 (or IPv6, depending) address returned by `hostname -I` is used. This is used because under some dual stack networking setups (especially under Podman, looking at you pasta), only the v4 address will be written to `/etc/hosts`. At this point, if `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` still isn't set, an error is thrown that no valid IP could be found. `hostname -I` doesn't output a stable order, but containers often will only have a single IP address. In a container connected to multiple networks, there isn't a sure way to figure out the correct public IP automatically, which is why `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` isn't overwritten. ## Enhanced FDB_COORDINATOR ip resolution ### Issue FDB Coordinator discovery always looks up IPv4 addresses, as `dig` by default searches for A records. It also doesn't respect the local `/etc/hosts` file. ### New Behavior Based on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, fdb coordinator ip is discovered with either `getent ahostsv4` or `getent ahostsv6`. This will prefer the local hosts file if it has the name, otherwise it will try to reach a remote DNS server.

signals.title: Move storage simulation capabilities out of `fdbrpc`
signals.text: ## Summary Follow up on #13080 and #13180 by moving the storage/TSS capability API out of the generic simulator policy. - Define `FDBSimulationCapability` and `IFDBSimulationPolicy` in `fdbclient`, and implement the interface in the existing server-owned `FDBSimulationPolicy`. - Query the currently installed, reference-counted simulation policy. Missing or non-FDB policies keep all capabilities disabled, and policy replacement cannot leave a stale provider. - Preserve the existing live TSS-mode predicates, mismatch severity, and fault-injection behavior. No protocol, serialization, scheduling, or random-draw changes are intended. - Document each policy implementation and keep focused regression coverage for fail-closed defaults and reentrant policy lifetime. ## Testing ### Current focused validation - Compiled and linked `fdbclient_test`; the build wrapper returned a nonzero status after linking. - Remaining client capability tests (`Defaults` and `ReentrantReplacement`): 2/2 passed in both normal and simulated modes with seed 13902. - Clang-format and `git diff --check` passed. ### Earlier validation - Existing TSS comparison, load-balancing hook, and `waitValueOrSignal` tests: 6/6 passed in both modes. - Compiled and linked `fdbrpclinktest`, `fdbclient_test`, `fdbrpc_test`, `fdbserver_core_test`, and `fdbserver`; executed the independent RPC link test successfully. - Two unchanged `tests/fast/CycleTest.toml` runs with BUGGIFY off and fault injection on: all four test phases passed, with no severity-40 trace events. - Clang-format 19 and `git diff --check` passed. The simulation runs selected normal and mutation-dropping TSS configurations, but neither completed TSS pairing. They provide general integration coverage, not proof of active TSS request comparison or injected faults; the retained focused tests cover fail-closed capability dispatch and reentrant policy lifetime directly.

signals.title: Add optional object key prefix support to blobstore backups
signals.text: ## Problem Blobstore backup containers currently place backup data under `data/<name>/...` and their index entries under `backups/<name>` at the bucket root. This prevents operators from placing all objects belonging to an FDB backup under one deployment-specific key prefix for prefix-scoped IAM policies, replication rules, lifecycle policies, inventory, cleanup, and cost accounting. ## Solution Add an optional `prefix` parameter to blobstore backup URLs: ```text blobstore://<host>/<name>?bucket=<bucket>&prefix=<key_prefix> ``` With `prefix=p`, the layout becomes: ```text p/data/<name>/... p/backups/<name> ``` This change: - parses and validates the parameter in `BackupContainerBlobStore`; - uses the prefix consistently for data reads/writes/lists/deletes and index create/exists/delete operations; - makes container listing enumerate the prefixed index tree and return reopenable URLs carrying the same parameter; - applies the same path construction to BulkDump/BulkLoad data, consuming the parameter after materializing it in the direct object URL; and - documents the URL syntax, compatibility requirements, and overlap semantics. The parameter is optional. When it is absent, the existing object key layout is unchanged. `file://` and `azure://` containers are unaffected. Prefix values have leading and trailing `/` characters stripped. After that normalization, `/` separates path segments; each segment is limited to ASCII `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, internal empty segments and `.` or `..` segments are rejected, and the first segment cannot be the reserved `data` or `backups` folder. If normalization leaves an empty value, the existing bucket-root layout is used. The prefix only changes object-key construction; FoundationDB does not enforce isolation between other overlapping layouts. Any security boundary must be enforced by the object store/IAM configuration. Prefix/name combinations that result in overlapping object trees must be avoided; behavior is undefined. BulkDump/BulkLoad URL derivation now uses the canonical blobstore URL parser. Malformed blobstore URLs therefore raise `backup_invalid_url` with the existing `BlobStoreEndpointBadURL` diagnostic instead of the helper's previous `std::invalid_argument`. ## Testing - `bin/fdbclient_test -f '/backup/containers/blobstore/prefix'` - `bin/fdbclient_test -f '/bulkload/getBackupDataPath/prefix'` - `ctest -R '^dir_backup_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^blob_backup_restore_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^blob_backup_restore_prefix_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^s3_backup_bulkdump_bulkload_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^s3_backup_bulkdump_bulkload_prefix_tests$' --output-on-failure` - Sphinx HTML build with warnings treated as errors - Prefixed rangefile backup/restore against Tencent COS through its S3-compatible API: 8/8 checks passed (physical layout, list isolation, and restored-data equality) - Prefixed rangefile backup/restore against Alibaba Cloud OSS through its S3-compatible API: 8/8 checks passed (physical layout, list isolation, and restored-data equality) Joshua/simulation was not run. The changed behavior is in blobstore URL and object-path handling and is covered by focused unit tests plus MockS3 and real S3-compatible end-to-end tests. Performance testing was not run. Prefix parsing occurs on container-open/list and BulkDump/BulkLoad job-setup paths, not on per-object I/O paths. ## Discussion The corresponding Forum proposal is pending moderator approval for a newly registered account. Its public URL will be added here when available.

signals.title: Fix a use-after-free in S3Client copyUpFile() when it is cancelled
signals.text: Problem: copyUpFile() handed file->read() a raw pointer into a state vector that lives in the actor frame, so cancelling it mid-read freed the buffer while the read could still be writing to it. IAsyncFile.h says dropping a pending read on cancel is up to the implementation, so we can't count on it stopping by itself. Solution: hold each part's buffer in a shared_ptr and wrap the read in uncancellable(holdWhile(...)). This is the same pattern already used in calculateFileChecksum() in this file (from https://github.com/apple/foundationdb/pull/13871, now also on release-7.4). So overall, copyUpFile() stays cancellable, it just no longer owns the memory the read is writing to. I found this during a 7.4 audit while checking whether the upload-part path was fully cancellation-safe after #13871 fixed the checksum side. It's not portable from upstream main, because main only fixed this incidentally as part of a much larger unrelated rework, so this is a 7.4 only fix. Testing: - general 100K: baseline 99999/100000, fix 100000/100000 (zero severity-40 events on the fix side) - BulkDumping 10K: baseline 10000/10000, fix 10000/10000

signals.title: BulkLoad: split an unplaceable bulkload task instead of failing the restore
signals.text: A bulkload data move needs a destination team disjoint from `src`, and `src` is the union of the owners of every shard the task's range spans. A range spread across enough of the fleet therefore has no legal destination team at all. Re-attempting cannot clear it: every attempt presents the same range and recomputes the same source set. The relocator gives up at `stuckCount == 50`, the task is marked `Error`, and the restore fails. (Even though bulkload pulls from s3, it piggybacks on the fetchKeys mechanism; 'src' here is usually an empty shard on a server and then 'dest' are the servers receiving the datamove with the pull from s3 inlined with fetchKeys. Later we should try unhitching bulkload from fetchKeys. Until then we have this src vs dest clash to deal with. Attempts at making it so src and dest could overlap kept running into noops as the SS reasoned no need for a datamove -- the data is already at its destination). Measured on a 100M-record validation cluster (~40 storage servers): ``` DDBulkLoadEngineTaskGetTeamFailedToFindValidTeam TeamSize=200 DuplicatedCount=200 ValidTeamSize=0 UnhealthyTeamCount=0 NotEligibileTeamCount=0 ``` Every candidate team rejected, every one of them for source overlap — not health, not disk, not anything transient. Two consecutive validation runs failed this way. Note this is *not* the failure `#13873` addresses. That one is a destination team lost mid-flight, which is retryable and goes through re-dispatch. This one is no destination team being findable at selection time, which never reaches re-dispatch at all — `RestartCount` is 0 throughout. ## Fix When a task cannot be placed, narrow it instead of failing it: split the manifest list in two and replace the task with two tasks covering the same manifests over halves of its range. Fewer shards per task means a smaller source set, and at some granularity a disjoint team exists. Three things make this safe: - **No window where a range is unowned.** The children's ranges are derived from the *parent's* range, so they tile it exactly and the two `krmSetRange` writes overwrite the parent with no gap. Nothing is ever persisted in an invalid state. (Deriving them from the manifests' span instead is wrong: a task's range is its manifests' span intersected with the job range, so a clipped parent would get children reaching outside it.) - **Bounded without a counter.** Halving terminates: a task holding one manifest cannot be narrowed, and such a range is genuinely unplaceable and still marked `Error`, with a trace saying why. - **A range owned by several tasks is now a legitimate state.** `bulkLoadJobFindTask` reports it as its own outcome rather than folding it into "found" or "not found", because the two callers need opposite things: a monitor must stop, while the executor must *not* treat the range as unclaimed — creating a task there would overwrite the narrower ones with a task exactly as wide as the range that could not be placed. Also included, and reachable independently of splitting: `bulkLoadJobMonitorTask` rethrew `actor_cancelled` without releasing its parallelism slot. Cancellation is how the job manager tears monitors down when it restarts, so each restart permanently shrank the budget until `scheduleBulkLoadJob` blocked forever waiting for a slot no live monitor held — a bulkload job that stops progressing with no error logged anywhere. This is pre-existing and can be split out if reviewers prefer. ## Validation - **100M cluster run, end to end, audit passed** — the bulkload restore's contents matched an independent rangefile restore of the same backup. 400 `GetTeamFailedToFindValidTeam` events, 8 tasks split, 6 monitors taking the new stop-monitoring path, 0 tasks reaching `Error`, 0 job-manager restarts. The same cluster shape and workload failed twice before this change. - **Joshua** found a bug in an earlier revision of this patch — the manifest-span derivation described above, which tripped its own tiling assertion on four seeds of `BulkDumpingS3WithChaos`. Fixed here; those four seeds now pass with the split path still exercised. - `BulkLoadingDestTeamFailure` and `BulkLoadingDestTeamFailureExhausted` pass; the latter now enters the split path and declines (its workload's tasks hold a single manifest), falling through to the existing `Error` behaviour unchanged. ## Not included A simulation test that reproduces the condition exists but is held back: it needs shard-size knobs extreme enough that the bulkdump exceeds the test's own `bulkdump_job_timeout`, which is a separate problem in the backup path. It will follow once that is addressed. This is the honest boundary of this fix: it rescues a task whose range spans several manifests, which is the case measured at 100M and above. It does nothing for a single wide manifest, where the only remedies are more capacity, a finer dump, or relaxing the destination-team disjointness requirement itself.

signals.title: Backup: log the bulkdump timeout that was actually used

signals.title: Wait for GRV before injecting in-flight commit timeouts

The injected timeout previously returned while the detached commit helper could still be waiting for its read version. A self-conflicting retry could therefore commit before the original attempt acquired its read version, defeating the retry's guarantee that earlier attempts cannot commit afterward. Waiting for GRV before starting the detached helper preserves that guarantee. Normal execution with client-buggify disabled is unchanged. ## Validation - The regression fails on the unfixed implementation because commit completes while the GRV gate is still closed. - The fixed regression passes in native and simulated unit-runner modes, covering GRV errors, transaction cancellation, commit-future cancellation, and disabling the timeout during the GRV wait, with RYW both enabled and disabled. - All seven existing WriteMap unit tests pass. - `CApiCancelTransactionWithTimeout` passes ten fresh-cluster runs. The blocking, callback, and database-per-transaction cancellation cases also pass. ## Scope This is a pre-existing client failure-injection defect, investigated following the C API test failure on #13699. signals.title: Backport #12440 and #12464 to release-7.4: fix ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob short-circuiting shadowed knob overrides
signals.text: Backports the two-commit "5s fuzzing" series from `main` to `release-7.4`: - **#12440** `05d36e167d` — fuzz the read transaction-life window in simulation - **#12464** `596f4cba6d` — fuzz the write window, and **fix `ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob` short-circuiting** The second commit is the one that matters here. `main` has had this since 2025-11-05; `release-7.4` never got either commit. The second commit fixes nightly 7.4 failures: ``` | fast/DataLossRecovery.toml | 3630903977 | 1 | | fast/DataLossRecovery.toml | 1937341837 | 1 | ``` ## The bug on release-7.4 `ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob` short circuited: ```cpp return clientKnobCollection.trySetKnob(knobName, knobValue) || knobValue.visitSetKnob(knobName, serverKnobs); ``` For a knob name declared in **both** `ClientKnobs` and `ServerKnobs`, the client copy is assigned, `true` is returned, and `serverKnobs` is never touched — while `setKnob` reports success. On `release-7.4` that affects `MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS`, `VERSIONS_PER_SECOND`, `GLOBAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_TIMEOUT` and `FASTRESTORE_ATOMICOP_WEIGHT`. Because every override path funnels through `IKnobCollection::setKnob`, this also silently broke `--knob-...` on a real `fdbserver`, not just simulation. ## How it surfaced `tests/fast/DataLossRecovery.toml` sets both transaction-life windows to 5s specifically to defeat BUGGIFY — its comment describes this exact failure mode. Only the read knob got through: ``` fdbserver -r simulation -f tests/fast/DataLossRecovery.toml -s 3630903977 -b on ``` 4 SevErrors; one real, three cascading: | # | Type | Error | |---|------|-------| | 1 | `TestFailure` (Workload=DataLossRecovery) | **`start_move_keys_too_many_retries`** (1250) | | 2 | `StartFailedForWorkloadDataLossRecovery` | `operation_failed` | | 3 | `RunTests` | `operation_failed` | | 4 | `SetupAndRunError` | `operation_failed` | From the trace: at t=0 there are **three** relevant `Knob` lines — `max_read...=1000000` (ServerKnobs, buggified), `max_write...=5000000` (ClientKnobs) **and** `max_write...=1000000` (ServerKnobs, buggified). At t=1 `AssignKnobValue` sets read to 5000000 (reaches `SERVER_KNOBS`) and write to 5000000 (a no-op on the client copy). So the read window was 5s as intended while the **write window stayed at the buggified 1s**. The resolver rejects commits whose read snapshot is older than `commitVersion - MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS` (`Resolver.actor.cpp:339` → `SkipList.cpp:837`). One `startMoveKeys` transaction takes ~2.4s on a 45-machine simulated cluster, so every attempt blew the 1s window; 50 retries then `start_move_keys_too_many_retries` (`MoveKeys.actor.cpp:1193`). Confirming evidence, which rules out a sick cluster: a single `MasterRecoveryState` sequence at t=5.59 ending `fully_recovered` with nothing during the failure window; ratekeeper idle (`TPSLimit` mostly `1e+09`, `WorstStorageServerVersionLag=0`); and decisively, `ResolverMetrics.TransactionsTooOld` on the system-keyspace resolver climbing `40 → 44 → 51 → … → 99` across t=102→187 while **every other resolver reports 0** for the entire run. With the read window correctly at 5s, 2.4s transactions could not have failed on reads — it is the write window. Three other tests were also silently not getting the server-side value they ask for: `tests/slow/GcGenerations.toml`, `tests/fast/EncryptedBackupCorrectness.toml`, `tests/negative/ResolverIgnoreTooOld.toml`. ## Adaptations from upstream Neither commit applies cleanly. Two deliberate deviations, both noted in the commit messages: **1. Knob declaration layout.** `release-7.4` declares the transaction-life-version knobs in their original positions — `ClientKnobs.cpp` beside the backup knobs, `ServerKnobs.cpp` below `ENABLE_VERSION_VECTOR` (because `buggifyShortReadWindow` depended on it). `main` hoisted both into a dedicated "knobs that control 5s timeout" section. signals.title: Add throughput-aware native CDC tag placement and live retagging
signals.text: ## Summary - Add opt-in, data-distributor-owned sampling of producer write load for native CDC tag placement. Fresh, generation-matched samples guide registration; incomplete or stale comparisons fall back to stream counts. - Select bounded, paced, overlap-aware live moves between tags owned by the same CDC proxy or an unused tag. Revalidate the assignment snapshot and data-distributor lock in the mutation transaction. - Use the retag transaction's actual commit version as the routing boundary, reconcile proxy histories in place, and retain old-tag history until durable acknowledgement permits canonicalization and retired-pop cleanup. - Add policy, codec, proxy, live-retagging, and disabled-restart coverage; document the protocol and rollout boundary. ## Safety and rollout `NATIVE_CDC_TAG_BALANCING_ENABLED` defaults to `false`. Sampling has stream/shard/concurrency/deadline bounds, moves have cooldown and minimum-improvement gates, and each stream has at most one pending move. A pending history row preserves the existing key layout and stores a commit versionstamp in its value. Old-tag reads end before that committed cutover; target-tag reads start there. Delivery is bounded by a validated metadata read version, preventing an older routing snapshot from skipping target-tag data. After acknowledgement, cleanup restores a single empty-valued history row and retains the old tag's recovery-safe pop obligation. Pending-history finalization continues with admission or balancing disabled, independently of the sampling stream limit. This PR does not implement cross-proxy load balancing or establish a production throughput/stream-count envelope. Before enabling balancing, all CDC-serving and recovery binaries must understand commit-stamped histories; the existing `withNativeCdc` capability alone does not negotiate that support. Before returning to pre-retag CDC binaries, stop new moves and finalize or remove pending transitions. Disabling the knob alone is not sufficient for that downgrade. ## Validation - [x] clang-format 19.1.7, whitespace checks, and the three new TOML configurations. - [x] `fdbclient_test -f /SystemData/NativeCDC`: 1 passed. - [x] `fdbclient_test -f /NativeCDC/`: 5 passed. - [x] `fdbserver_cdcproxy_test -f /NativeCDC/`: 13 passed. - [x] `fdbserver_logsystem_test -f /NativeCDC/`: 6 passed. - [x] `fdbserver_datadistributor_test -f /NativeCDC/TagBalancing/`: 6 passed. - [x] Full `fdbserver` build with Clang 19.1.5. - [x] `NativeCdcThroughputRetagging`: seeds 1, 2, and 3. - [x] Paired `NativeCdcRetagDisableRestart`: seeds 11/12 and 21/22. - [x] Existing CDC regressions at seed 42: EndToEnd, AssignmentPublication, SharedTag, RetiredSharedTagSnapshot, MemoryBound, ReplyChunking, OversizedPeek, DurableAckScan, RetiredRecovery, RetiredRecoveryMultiRegion, Satellite, and the DisableRestart pair (resumed at seed 43). All 31 focused unit tests and 17 simulation runs passed. The simulation configurations disable buggify; EndToEnd and Satellite retain their configured fault injection. The remaining scenarios use their explicit failure/recovery actions. The live-retagging workload uses real producer writes, verifies complete unacknowledged replay in fresh delivery epochs, and checks repeated movement, shared-tag retention, and a write between the retag read version and commit. The restart pair requires both sides of a pending cutover to drain and finalize while admission and balancing are disabled. No production benchmark or mixed-version rollout qualification is claimed.

signal.title: (Backport to 7.4): DD finishMoveKeys: move waitForShardReady outside transaction (#13364)
signal.text: Backport 0887ae6d29 from main to release-7.4 ``` ## Backport notes - Branch `release-7.4` uses Flow actors (`.actor.cpp`, `state` keyword, `wait()` macro) rather than main's C++20 coroutines (`co_await`). Local variables that need to cross a `wait()` point are declared with `state`; return statements use `return`, not `co_return`. - `constexpr` is not compatible with `state` variables on 7.4. - Otherwise the change is behavior-identical to the main PR. ``` DD finishMove*: drop the transaction across waitForShardReady SERVER_READY_QUORUM_TIMEOUT (15s) was used inside a transaction with a ~5s lifetime (MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS). When destination servers were slow to respond, the wait alone consumed the txn budget, and commits failed with transaction_too_old — retries too, cascading into the DD pipeline stalls observed in incidents. Restructure both finish-move functions (finishMoveKeys / finishMoveShards, dispatched on SHARD_ENCODE_LOCATION_METADATA) into a two-transaction pattern with the wait in between: Transaction 1: read keyServers / serverTags / serverList (and dataMove metadata for finishMoveShards) via the new readShardState() helper. Save the read version and drop the transaction (tr.reset()). Wait: waitForShardReady — runs OUTSIDE any transaction; the 15s timeout is now safe. Transaction 2: re-verify via destUnchanged() (dest hasn't changed, dataMove still in Running phase for finishMoveShards), then commit metadata writes. If the destination changed during the wait, the inner loop retries from the top — same as today's behaviour on transient errors, just without burning the txn budget on the wait itself. Verification & retry details: * destUnchanged() loops every sub-range, not just keyServers[0]. The keys-flavor (`expectedDataMoveId={}`) tolerates empty-dest entries whose src ⊆ expectedDest — matching the planning loop's `alreadyMoved = dest2.empty() && isSubset` branch, which lets sibling iterations of OUR move that already completed pass through. A foreign src on an empty-dest entry signals a different move owns the range and forces a retry to avoid clobbering it. The shards-flavor uses the dataMoveId stamp as the per-sub-range invariant. * All retry paths (dest-changed, data-move-deleted, phase-changed, plus the count-mismatch else-branch in finishMoveShards) are bounded by FINISH_MOVE_KEYS_MAX_RETRIES and back off via finishMoveKeysBackoff(). Without the cap the dest-changed branch could livelock; the shards- side count-mismatch path was previously unbounded. * Txn 2's writes use the post-wait snapshot: keyServersValue uses reread.uidToTagMap; finishMoveShards introduces a postWaitDataMove local so the partial-complete / deleteCheckpoints / dataMoveValue writes reflect the fresh dataMove state. * runPreCheck=false is set inline on each retry path. The partial-complete success-continue deliberately leaves runPreCheck alone so chunks 2..N of a multi-transaction move each get their own AUDIT_DATAMOVE_PRE_CHECK. * finishMoveShards now takes finishMoveKeysParallelismLock per iteration (mirroring finishMoveKeys). signal.title: Add optional object key prefix support to blobstore backups
signal.text: ## Problem Blobstore backup containers currently place backup data under `data/<name>/...` and their index entries under `backups/<name>` at the bucket root. This prevents operators from placing all objects belonging to an FDB backup under one deployment-specific key prefix for prefix-scoped IAM policies, replication rules, lifecycle policies, inventory, cleanup, and cost accounting. ## Solution Add an optional `prefix` parameter to blobstore backup URLs: ```text blobstore://<host>/<name>?bucket=<bucket>&prefix=<key_prefix> ``` With `prefix=p`, the layout becomes: ```text p/data/<name>/... p/backups/<name> ``` This change: - parses and validates the parameter in `BackupContainerBlobStore`; - uses the prefix consistently for data reads/writes/lists/deletes and index create/exists/delete operations; - makes container listing enumerate the prefixed index tree and return reopenable URLs carrying the same parameter; - applies the same path construction to BulkDump/BulkLoad data, consuming the parameter after materializing it in the direct object URL; and - documents the URL syntax, compatibility requirements, and overlap semantics. The parameter is optional. When it is absent, the existing object key layout is unchanged. `file://` and `azure://` containers are unaffected. Prefix values have leading and trailing `/` characters stripped. After that normalization, `/` separates path segments; each segment is limited to ASCII `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, internal empty segments and `.` or `..` segments are rejected, and the first segment cannot be the reserved `data` or `backups` folder. If normalization leaves an empty value, the existing bucket-root layout is used. The prefix only changes object-key construction; FoundationDB does not enforce isolation between other overlapping layouts. Any security boundary must be enforced by the object store/IAM configuration. Prefix/name combinations that result in overlapping object trees must be avoided; behavior is undefined. BulkDump/BulkLoad URL derivation now uses the canonical blobstore URL parser. Malformed blobstore URLs therefore raise `backup_invalid_url` with the existing `BlobStoreEndpointBadURL` diagnostic instead of the helper's previous `std::invalid_argument`. ## Testing - `bin/fdbclient_test -f '/backup/containers/blobstore/prefix'` - `bin/fdbclient_test -f '/bulkload/getBackupDataPath/prefix'` - `ctest -R '^dir_backup_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^blob_backup_restore_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^blob_backup_restore_prefix_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^s3_backup_bulkdump_bulkload_tests$' --output-on-failure` - `ctest -R '^s3_backup_bulkdump_bulkload_prefix_tests$' --output-on-failure` - Sphinx HTML build with warnings treated as errors - Prefixed rangefile backup/restore against Tencent COS through its S3-compatible API: 8/8 checks passed (physical layout, list isolation, and restored-data equality) - Prefixed rangefile backup/restore against Alibaba Cloud OSS through its S3-compatible API: 8/8 checks passed (physical layout, list isolation, and restored-data equality) Joshua/simulation was not run. The changed behavior is in blobstore URL and object-path handling and is covered by focused unit tests plus MockS3 and real S3-compatible end-to-end tests. Performance testing was not run. Prefix parsing occurs on container-open/list and BulkDump/BulkLoad job-setup paths, not on per-object I/O paths. ## Discussion The corresponding Forum proposal is pending moderator approval for a newly registered account. Its public URL will be added here when available.

signal.title: Fix a use-after-free in S3Client copyUpFile() when it is cancelled
signal.text: Problem: copyUpFile() handed file->read() a raw pointer into a state vector that lives in the actor frame, so cancelling it mid-read freed the buffer while the read could still be writing to it. IAsyncFile.h says dropping a pending read on cancel is up to the implementation, so we can't count on it stopping by itself. Solution: hold each part's buffer in a shared_ptr and wrap the read in uncancellable(holdWhile(...)). This is the same pattern already used in calculateFileChecksum() in this file (from https://github.com/apple/foundationdb/pull/13871, now also on release-7.4). So overall, copyUpFile() stays cancellable, it just no longer owns the memory the read is writing to. I found this during a 7.4 audit while checking whether the upload-part path was fully cancellation-safe after #13871 fixed the checksum side. It's not portable from upstream main, because main only fixed this incidentally as part of a much larger unrelated rework, so this is a 7.4 only fix. Testing: - general 100K: baseline 99999/100000, fix 100000/100000 (zero severity-40 events on the fix side) - BulkDumping 10K: baseline 10000/10000, fix 10000/10000

signal.title: Wait for a read version before simulating in-flight commit timeouts
signal.text: ## Summary The client-buggify in-flight commit path reports `transaction_timed_out` immediately after launching its uncancellable helper, even when that helper is still waiting for a read version. A self-conflicting retry can then finish before the older attempt acquires its read version, so the successful retry no longer fences that attempt. Wait for the read version before launching the helper and reporting the synthetic timeout in both RYW commit branches. The unbuggified path is unchanged. Extend the existing disconnected-timeout suite with forced client-buggify coverage for RYW enabled and disabled. Without a read version, a commit must wait for its real timeout rather than report an injected in-flight timeout immediately. ## Validation - Regression-only control: both new subcases fail on the original implementation, returning in less than 0.2 ms instead of the configured 500 ms; all 12 existing cases pass. - Fixed GCC Release build: local and external-client disconnected suites each pass 13 cases and 31 assertions. The local-client run supplies the red-before-green proof; the external-client run is compatibility coverage. - Focused `fdbclient_test` WriteMap tests: 7 passed, 0 failed. - All five connected `CApiCancelTransaction` CTests pass: blocking, callback, per-transaction database, TLS, and timeout variants. - `fdb_c_api_test_CApiCancelTransactionWithTimeout` passes 20 additional consecutive runs with client buggify enabled.

signal.title: [release-7.3] always increment finishedQueries counter if incrementing allQueries
signal.text: Storage server processes publish a pair of counters `total_queries` and `finished_queries` (as well as a derived special counter `query_queue_max`) tracking how many read operations have been started and finished (and the high-water-mark for the number of pending queries—those that have been started, but not finished—in a status-fetch interval). Unfortunately, the counter underlying `total_queries` was incremented at the beginning of one of several actors, and the matching increment to `finished_queries` was done at the end, with several intervening `wait`s. If the actor was cancelled (or experienced another non-returnable error), `finished_queries` was not incremented, resulting in a permanent drift between `total_queries` and `all_queries` and apparently endless growth in `query_queue_max`. The easiest way to demonstrate this behavior is to have two different clients alternate between setting watches and updating values for the same keys—for example, run two simultaneous instances of this [simple Java program](https://gist.github.com/jkt-signal/1c3ea2a4a6aafd51571b462c57b50fd9) against a single database, and monitor its status to see `query_queue_max` on storage servers go up permanently every time you run the test. To solve this problem, we add a simple class `CountedSection` to `flow/Stats.h` to bump two counters in RAII-enforced balance; once a local `CountedSection` has bumped the first counter, it will always eventually bump the second one whether it is destroyed as a result of normal exit or exception. (Of course, if you store one in a heap object and leak it, you will still experience drift, so, uh, don't do that.) `CountedSection` is made move-only so you can use it in actor state, since `state` variables seem to always be default-constructed and then assigned to their initializers even if the initialization comes before the first `wait` in an actor. One of the actors involved actually updates a second counter pair, `getMappedRangeQueries` and `finishedGetMappedRangeQueries`, in a way vulnerable to the same problem, so we use `CountedSection` to address that as well, though I have not seen any instances of these getting out of sync (entirely due to lack of trying). Some other metrics updated at the ends of the affected actors—mostly latency metrics, but also some tagged size distributions—are not addressed by this change. Arguably they should not be, since including latency and response size of interrupted queries may significantly throw off the statistics in a not-necessarily-useful way. Leaving this as an RFC because I'm not sufficiently familiar with the FoundationDB testing setup to write a good test; the Java program linked above is a great demonstration but is not trivially adapted to an integration test (and presumably we'd like tests of the fdbserver itself to be C++, not dependent on the Java bindings). Advice for how to test the change greatly appreciated! This PR is against the 7.3 branch, rather than `main`, because all the relevant actors have been rewritten to use C++20 standard coroutines in the interim, and while I strongly suspect the same bug applies equally in `main`, I was not able to confirm this because `main` does not currently build a usable fdb for me. Porting forward to `main` should be relatively trivial and I'm happy to do so if requested.

signal.title: Backport #12440 and #12464 to release-7.4: fix ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob short-circuiting shadowed knob overrides
signal.text: Backports the two-commit "5s fuzzing" series from `main` to `release-7.4`: - **#12440** `05d36e167d` — fuzz the read transaction-life window in simulation - **#12464** `596f4cba6d` — fuzz the write window, and **fix `ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob` short-circuiting** The second commit is the one that matters here. `main` has had this since 2025-11-05; `release-7.4` never got either commit. The second commit fixes nightly 7.4 failures: ``` | fast/DataLossRecovery.toml | 3630903977 | 1 | | fast/DataLossRecovery.toml | 1937341837 | 1 | ``` ## The bug on release-7.4 `ServerKnobCollection::trySetKnob` short circuited: ```cpp return clientKnobCollection.trySetKnob(knobName, knobValue) || knobValue.visitSetKnob(knobName, serverKnobs); ``` For a knob name declared in **both** `ClientKnobs` and `ServerKnobs`, the client copy is assigned, `true` is returned, and `serverKnobs` is never touched — while `setKnob` reports success. On `release-7.4` that affects `MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS`, `VERSIONS_PER_SECOND`, `GLOBAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_TIMEOUT` and `FASTRESTORE_ATOMICOP_WEIGHT`. Because every override path funnels through `IKnobCollection::setKnob`, this also silently broke `--knob-...` on a real `fdbserver`, not just simulation. ## How it surfaced `tests/fast/DataLossRecovery.toml` sets both transaction-life windows to 5s specifically to defeat BUGGIFY — its comment describes this exact failure mode. Only the read knob got through: ``` fdbserver -r simulation -f tests/fast/DataLossRecovery.toml -s 3630903977 -b on ``` 4 SevErrors; one real, three cascading: | # | Type | Error | |---|------|-------| | 1 | `TestFailure` (Workload=DataLossRecovery) | **`start_move_keys_too_many_retries`** (1250) | | 2 | `StartFailedForWorkloadDataLossRecovery` | `operation_failed` | | 3 | `RunTests` | `operation_failed` | | 4 | `SetupAndRunError` | `operation_failed` | From the trace: at t=0 there are **three** relevant `Knob` lines — `max_read...=1000000` (ServerKnobs, buggified), `max_write...=5000000` (ClientKnobs) **and** `max_write...=1000000` (ServerKnobs, buggified). At t=1 `AssignKnobValue` sets read to 5000000 (reaches `SERVER_KNOBS`) and write to 5000000 (a no-op on the client copy). So the read window was 5s as intended while the **write window stayed at the buggified 1s**. The resolver rejects commits whose read snapshot is older than `commitVersion - MAX_WRITE_TRANSACTION_LIFE_VERSIONS` (`Resolver.actor.cpp:339` → `SkipList.cpp:837`). One `startMoveKeys` transaction takes ~2.4s on a 45-machine simulated cluster, so every attempt blew the 1s window; 50 retries then `start_move_keys_too_many_retries` (`MoveKeys.actor.cpp:1193`). Confirming evidence, which rules out a sick cluster: a single `MasterRecoveryState` sequence at t=5.59 ending `fully_recovered` with nothing during the failure window; ratekeeper idle (`TPSLimit` mostly `1e+09`, `WorstStorageServerVersionLag=0`); and decisively, `ResolverMetrics.TransactionsTooOld` on the system-keyspace resolver climbing `40 → 44 → 51 → … → 99` across t=102→187 while **every other resolver reports 0** for the entire run. With the read window correctly at 5s, 2.4s transactions could not have failed on reads — it is the write window. Three other tests were also silently not getting the server-side value they ask for: `tests/slow/GcGenerations.toml`, `tests/fast/EncryptedBackupCorrectness.toml`, `tests/negative/ResolverIgnoreTooOld.toml`. ## Adaptations from upstream Neither commit applies cleanly. Two deliberate deviations, both noted in the commit messages: **1. Knob declaration layout.** `release-7.4` declares the transaction-life-version knobs in their original positions — `ClientKnobs.cpp` beside the backup knobs, `ServerKnobs.cpp` below `ENABLE_VERSION_VECTOR` (because `buggifyShortReadWindow` depended on it). `main` hoisted both into a dedicated "knobs that control 5s timeout" section. The value changes are applied **in place** rather than moving declarations, to keep the diff reviewable. The now-unused `buggifyShortReadWindow` local is deleted, as upstream did. **2. Include churn dropped.** #12464 also removed includes from `ClientKnobs.cpp` (`FDBTypes.h`, `SystemData.h`, `Tenant.h`) and `ServerKnobs.cpp` (`CompressionUtils.h`, `flow.h`), compensating elsewhere with `fdbrpc.h` in `WaitFailure.actor.cpp` and `TDMetric.actor.h` in `BulkLoading.h`. **None of that is applied here.** `release-7.4`'s `ServerKnobs.cpp` still calls `CompressionUtils::toString`/`getRandomFilter` for `BLOB_GRANULE_COMPRESSION_FILTER` — `main` no longer does — so dropping that include would break the build. And upstream's removal of `fdbrpc.h` from `ServerKnobs.h` only fixed up the transitive consumers that `main` happens to have; `release-7.4`'s set may differ. The cleanup is incidental to the fix, so this backport changes behaviour only. After the backport the three knob lines match `main` character-for-character. ## Behaviour change to be aware of Read-window fuzzing is now `getSimulatedTxnTimeoutSeconds()` (90% → 5s, else 1–10s) instead of the old BUGGIFY ladder, so `release-7.4` loses the `buggifyShortReadWindow` 0.1s case and the 10× case. Write-window fuzzing moves to `ClientKnobs` as the single source, with `ServerKnobs` taking its value from the client copy — so the two can no longer disagree. **`tests/negative/ResolverIgnoreTooOld.toml` is the one to watch**: it asks for a *shorter* 1s write window and until now was silently getting whatever BUGGIFY chose, so its override starts taking effect for the first time.

signal.title: Convert CoroFlow actors to standard C++ coroutines
signal.text: ## Summary Convert the Boost and libcoro CoroFlow implementations to regular `.cpp` files using standard C++ coroutines. Preserve the public thread-pool interface, task priorities, and stack-switch scheduling boundaries. The mechanical conversion exposed a pool-lifecycle slowdown. Complete the error watcher through a private shutdown signal, retain the pool across cancellation callbacks that may release its last owner, and keep implicit cleanup inside the coroutine's exception boundary. Use detached coroutines only for discarded fire-and-forget scheduling results. Failed explicit cleanup retains its existing implicit-cleanup retry. Add focused lifecycle/error tests and a production-linked `fdbserver_coroflow_bench` target. ## Validation - All 11 `/fdbserver/CoroFlow/` tests pass on both backends in Net2 and Sim2. Across the original implementation and four incremental coroutine variants, all 440 test executions pass. - SQLite-backed `CycleTest.toml` passes on both optimized backends with seed `20260818`, BUGGIFY, and fault injection enabled. - Formatting and `git diff --check` pass. ## Performance Compared with the actor implementation at the branch's [public base](https://github.com/apple/foundationdb/commit/368414496b3768aa2b4f09165bfd495dde781af9). Measured on Linux x86-64 with Clang 19.1.5, Release `-O3`, static libc++, LLD, and jemalloc; sanitizers and profiling disabled. The same `^coroflow_` benchmark harness was used for all variants in forward/reverse order on one pinned CPU, with nine repetitions per invocation and a one-second minimum for the main benchmarks. | Backend | Operation | Original actors | Mechanical conversion | Optimized | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | libcoro | Start/stop | 7.650 µs | 9.390 µs | 7.645 µs | | libcoro | Suspended wait | 1.663 µs | 1.698 µs | 1.687 µs | | Boost | Start/stop | 4.652 µs | 5.940 µs | 4.486 µs | | Boost | Suspended wait | 262.9 ns | 246.9 ns | 239.2 ns | Ready waits are effectively unchanged. The large start/stop regression is removed in this measurement, but the change is not performance-neutral everywhere: libcoro suspended waits remain 1.41% slower, and empty-pool create/drop costs approximately 153 ns more on libcoro and 247 ns more on Boost. These are focused microbenchmark results, not an end-to-end throughput or statistical-equivalence claim.

signal.title: Add ipv6 support to docker container
signal.text: Added functionality for `fdb.bash` to support ipv6, provided the new env variable `FDB_IP_VERSION` is set to 6 (or any string containing 6, such as v6, ipv6, iwantipv6, etc. ) There is an unfortunate caveat of no dual stack support, as FDB coordinators are recognized by their IP+port and not their machineid, to the best of my knowledge. If I'm wrong and FDB does not double count a coordinator with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in the cluster file, I would be happy to add dual stack support to this. This was part of now-split-up #13822, with slightly more robust logic. # Changes ## IPv6 Support ### Issue Before now, `fdb.bash` would throw an error if `hostname -i` resolved to a v6 address, as it would not be encased in brackets. ### New Behavior Depending on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, `fdb.bash` will try and find the machine's v4 or v6 address. IPv4 is the default pick. If `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` or `FDB_LISTEN_IP` are set, they will _not_ be overwritten. Otherwise, the first IPv4 (or IPv6, depending) address returned by `hostname -I` is used. This is used because under some dual stack networking setups (especially under Podman, looking at you pasta), only the v4 address will be written to `/etc/hosts`. At this point, if `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` still isn't set, an error is thrown that no valid IP could be found. `hostname -I` doesn't output a stable order, but containers often will only have a single IP address. In a container connected to multiple networks, there isn't a sure way to figure out the correct public IP automatically, which is why `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` isn't overwritten. ## Enhanced FDB_COORDINATOR ip resolution ### Issue FDB Coordinator discovery always looks up IPv4 addresses, as `dig` by default searches for A records. It also doesn't respect the local `/etc/hosts` file. ### New Behavior Based on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, fdb coordinator ip is discovered with either `getent ahostsv4` or `getent ahostsv6`. This will prefer the local hosts file if it has the name, otherwise it will try to reach a remote DNS server.

signal.text: ## Summary Keep ACTOR and C++20 coroutine versions of `BenchIONet2` in the same `fdbrpc_bench` binary for reproducible comparisons, and fix a remaining lifetime mismatch in the conversion. The ACTOR's `state Reference<IAsyncFile> f` survives loop iterations, so subsequent opens reuse the cached file. A loop-local coroutine handle instead closes the file after each iteration, causing another atomic create, rename, and directory sync. Both implementations now retain the file handle and child futures across iterations and use the same fixed seed. The coroutine child's existing `NoThrowOnCancel` behavior is unchanged. ## Measured results Release build with Clang 19.1.5, libc++, and `-O3`; no sanitizers or profiling. One binary contained ACTOR, the fixed coroutine, and a temporary unfixed coroutine differing only in file-handle lifetime. Six counterbalanced paired rounds produced 126 samples, each in a fresh process. Iteration counts matched across all three implementations at each size. The table reports **launched-child throughput per network-thread CPU second**. Gains compare the fixed and unfixed coroutines; ratios are medians of the six paired rounds. | Batch size | Iterations per sample | Throughput gain from fix | Fixed / ACTOR throughput | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 64 | +3.7% | 1.004x | | 8 | 64 | +34.7% | 1.000x | | 64 | 64 | +34.8% | 0.998x | | 512 | 64 | +29.9% | 0.991x | | 4,096 | 16 | +32.5% | 0.994x | | 32,768 | 8 | +22.5% | 0.720x | | 65,536 | 8 | +18.5% | 0.419x | The fix improved all 42 paired comparisons and restored approximate ACTOR parity through batch size 4,096. A substantial gap remains at the two largest sizes. At 65,536, the gain ranged from 17.7% to 20.2%, while fixed/ACTOR ranged from 0.377x to 0.568x. These are observed ranges, not confidence bounds. ## Validation - The final patch compiled successfully. ACTOR and coroutine smoke cases at sizes 1 and 65,536 passed (4/4). - A separate instrumented call-count check at size 512 with 16 iterations observed one atomic-file open, rename, and directory sync for ACTOR and the fixed coroutine, versus 16 of each for the unfixed coroutine. All three performed 16 data syncs. - The temporary unfixed variant and fixed-iteration controls were removed from the final patch. The instrumented call-count check and final smoke timings are excluded from the performance table. This fixes a benchmark-workload mismatch, not the entire large-batch slowdown. Retained backlog depends on both batch size and iteration count; extra I/O waits can allow more child CPU work to execute, and terminal child cancellation is outside the timed loop. These results do not isolate coroutine-creation cost, establish the cause of the remaining gap, or measure production performance. signal.title: Surface degraded multi-region status when failover is stuck waiting on the unavailable remote DC #12071
signal.text: **Surface degraded multi-region status when failover is stuck waiting on the unavailable remote DC** This PR introduces observability for #12071. Instead of preventing the stall where recovery waits for an unavailable remote datacenter, this change surfaces the stuck state to improve cluster visibility. ### Key Changes #### New Status Flag: `cluster.degraded_multi_region` The flag becomes `true` when all of the following conditions are met: - The cluster is configured with `usable_regions > 1`. - Recovery has progressed to or beyond the `accepting_commits` stage. - The remote region's log set cannot be recruited (signaled by `RemoteRegionLogsMissing` from `trackTlogRecovery`). - The state persists for longer than `DEGRADED_MULTI_REGION_MIN_STALL_SECONDS` (to avoid false positives during transient windows of normal non-initial recovery). #### New Trace Event - Added `ClusterControllerRecoveryRemoteRegionStall` for improved debugging and monitoring. #### Improved `fdbcli` Output - The data-loss warning is **softened** when `degraded_multi_region` is true, because committed data remains safe in the surviving region. - For empty `id` or `address` fields, the CLI now prints `"unknown"` instead of leaving them blank. #### Testing - **Simulation Test:** `DegradedMultiRegionStatus` – covers the stuck state and includes a false-positive check to ensure healthy recovery doesn't trigger the flag. - **Unit Tests:** Added for the new signal parsing logic. ### Why This Matters In a multi-region configuration, when one region fails, the second (surviving) region first recovers missing data from the **satellite of the first (failed) region**, which remains operational. After this data copy completes, recovery proceeds to the `accepting_commits` stage. However, at this point the recovery may stall because the failed region's logs remain unreachable. While this prevents the remote region from fully recovering, the surviving region continues to accept commits, and all committed data remains safe and consistent. The stall only affects the ability to restore the failed region, not the integrity of committed data. Previously, `fdbcli status` showed a misleading "potential data loss" warning. This PR replaces that with an honest representation of the **degraded but non-data-losing** state, providing clear visibility into the actual cluster condition. --- **Related Issue:** #12071 **Forum Discussion:** [link](https://forums.foundationdb.org/t/3dc2regions-simulating-primary-datacenter-failure/3329/18)

The injected timeout previously returned while the detached commit helper could still be waiting for its read version. The relevant implementation and test code are identical on that PR and main. The original CI missing-value failure did not reproduce in 21 ordinary attempts or 12 CPU-constrained concurrent attempts using its original binaries, so this change is not presented as conclusive attribution of that CI failure.

signal.title: BulkLoad: split an unplaceable bulkload task instead of failing the restore
signal.text: A bulkload data move needs a destination team disjoint from `src`, and `src` is the union of the owners of every shard the task's range spans. A range spread across enough of the fleet therefore has no legal destination team at all. Re-attempting cannot clear it: every attempt presents the same range and recomputes the same source set. The relocator gives up at `stuckCount == 50`, the task is marked `Error`, and the restore fails. (Even though bulkload pulls from s3, it piggybacks on the fetchKeys mechanism; 'src' here is usually an empty shard on a server and then 'dest' are the servers receiving the datamove with the pull from s3 inlined with fetchKeys. Later we should try unhitching bulkload from fetchKeys. Until then we have this src vs dest clash to deal with. Attempts at making it so src and dest could overlap kept running into noops as the SS reasoned no need for a datamove -- the data is already at its destination). Measured on a 100M-record validation cluster (~40 storage servers): ``` DDBulkLoadEngineTaskGetTeamFailedToFindValidTeam TeamSize=200 DuplicatedCount=200 ValidTeamSize=0 UnhealthyTeamCount=0 NotEligibileTeamCount=0 ``` Every candidate team rejected, every one of them for source overlap — not health, not disk, not anything transient. Two consecutive validation runs failed this way. Note this is *not* the failure `#13873` addresses. That one is a destination team lost mid-flight, which is retryable and goes through re-dispatch. This one is no destination team being findable at selection time, which never reaches re-dispatch at all — `RestartCount` is 0 throughout. ## Fix When a task cannot be placed, narrow it instead of failing it: split the manifest list in two and replace the task with two tasks covering the same manifests over halves of its range. Fewer shards per task means a smaller source set, and at some granularity a disjoint team exists. Three things make this safe: - **No window where a range is unowned.** The children's ranges are derived from the *parent's* range, so they tile it exactly and the two `krmSetRange` writes overwrite the parent with no gap. Nothing is ever persisted in an invalid state. (Deriving them from the manifests' span instead is wrong: a task's range is its manifests' span intersected with the job range, so a clipped parent would get children reaching outside it.) - **Bounded without a counter.** Halving terminates: a task holding one manifest cannot be narrowed, and such a range is genuinely unplaceable and still marked `Error`, with a trace saying why. - **A range owned by several tasks is now a legitimate state.** `bulkLoadJobFindTask` reports it as its own outcome rather than folding it into "found" or "not found", because the two callers need opposite things: a monitor must stop, while the executor must *not* treat the range as unclaimed — creating a task there would overwrite the narrower ones with a task exactly as wide as the range that could not be placed. Also included, and reachable independently of splitting: `bulkLoadJobMonitorTask` rethrew `actor_cancelled` without releasing its parallelism slot. Cancellation is how the job manager tears monitors down when it restarts, so each restart permanently shrank the budget until `scheduleBulkLoadJob` blocked forever waiting for a slot no live monitor held — a bulkload job that stops progressing with no error logged anywhere. This is pre-existing and can be split out if reviewers prefer. ## Validation - **100M cluster run, end to end, audit passed** — the bulkload restore's contents matched an independent rangefile restore of the same backup. 400 `GetTeamFailedToFindValidTeam` events, 8 tasks split, 6 monitors taking the new stop-monitoring path, 0 tasks reaching `Error`, 0 job-manager restarts. The same cluster shape and workload failed twice before this change. - **Joshua** found a bug in an earlier revision of this patch — the manifest-span derivation described above, which tripped its own tiling assertion on four seeds of `BulkDumpingS3WithChaos`. Fixed here; those four seeds now pass with the split path still exercised. - `BulkLoadingDestTeamFailure` and `BulkLoadingDestTeamFailureExhausted` pass; the latter now enters the split path and declines (its workload's tasks hold a single manifest), falling through to the existing `Error` behaviour unchanged. ## Not included A simulation test that reproduces the condition exists but is held back: it needs shard-size knobs extreme enough that the bulkdump exceeds the test's own `bulkdump_job_timeout`, which is a separate problem in the backup path. It will follow once that is addressed. This is the honest boundary of this fix: it rescues a task whose range spans several manifests, which is the case measured at 100M and above. It does nothing for a single wide manifest, where the only remedies are more capacity, a finer dump, or relaxing the destination-team disjointness requirement itself.

signal.title: Reduce coroutine overhead on storage-server paths
signal.text: ## Summary Reduce coroutine, allocation, and reference-counting overhead on the storage-server read/write and RPC paths: - Fast-path ready storage/MVCC and Redwood reads without constructing unnecessary coroutine frames or futures. - Cache ready Redwood page futures while preserving pending-future cancellation and lifetime behavior. - Return KAIO write completion directly as `Future<Void>`, avoiding an extra `success()` actor per disk write. - Reduce RPC serialization, `FutureStream`, `ActorCollection`, and detached-sender overhead. - Add focused regression and microbenchmark coverage. ## Performance Re-ran the full PR against main on 2026-08-21: clean main `9d4a14faf451` versus this PR's clean source state. **Observed throughput increased by 10.50% in this matched pair.** These results replace the earlier shorter-run measurements. Both runs used fresh three-process, single-redundancy `ssd-redwood-1` clusters (one stateless, one log, one storage process) on the same x86-64 host with 16 logical CPUs available. Builds used the same Release Clang 19.1.5/libc++/jemalloc configuration, with sanitizers and profiling disabled; source and fresh server/client binary provenance were verified for each revision. Mixed Mako `g18ui` workload: 18 GETs, one update, and one insert per transaction; 100,000 initial rows; 128-byte keys and 512-byte values; four load processes; seven run processes with 16 worker threads and 32 async workflows **per process** (224 workflows total), with no client TPS cap. Each run used `--warmup_seconds 300 --seconds 900`: approximately five minutes of excluded warmup followed by ten measured minutes. Inserts grow the dataset beyond the initial row count. | Revision | Measured TPS | Change vs. main | Conflicts | Errors / timeouts | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Main `9d4a14faf451` | 2,762.39 | — | 41,650 | 0 / 0 | | PR #13699 | **3,052.49** | **+10.50%** | 46,642 | 0 / 0 | Main completed 1,656,401 successful transactions in 599.626 measured seconds; the PR completed 1,830,287 in 599.604 seconds. Storage-server GET-query throughput rose from approximately 53.8k/s to 59.5k/s. Both runs saturated the storage main thread at approximately one CPU core, and every measured ratekeeper observation identified the storage write queue as the limiter. Mean storage queues remained high (approximately 944 MiB on main and 941 MiB on the PR). Mean durability lag was 84.7M versus 76.5M versions, but lag increased during both measurement windows. This is one sequential run per revision on a growing dataset under queue-limited saturation; it does not establish statistical confidence, low-lag steady-state capacity, or the contribution of any individual optimization. Sampled **full-run** latency means, including warmup, computed from exported latency sums/counts across all async workflows: | Operation | Main mean (ms) | PR mean (ms) | Change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | GET | 3.802 | 3.401 | -10.56% | | COMMIT | 3.075 | 3.369 | +9.55% | | TRANSACTION | 77.151 | 70.065 | -9.19% | Transaction and GET means improved in this pair, while the COMMIT mean increased.
